5.4 Supplementary analysis
Potential supplementary analyses include:

An unadjusted analysis, with or without stratification, to illustrate the impact of covariate adjustment on the point estimate and precision.
If the primary analysis is stratified, an unstratified analysis. Note that standard errors should account for stratified randomization even if the analysis is not stratified (Ye et al. 2024).
An analysis with a Cox PH model adjusted for covariates and stratified by randomization stratification factors, if the primary analysis is covariate-adjusted but marginal with respect to the covariates.
Estimates of different estimands, e.g., differences of the restricted mean survival times or differences of survival probabilities at landmark time points. Such analyses are particularly useful if the PH assumption is violated.

title: Missing covariates in RCTs - what to do, what to avoid, and what to prespecify
text:
Covariate adjustment is now standard for primary and key secondary analyses in confirmatory trials, supported by recent regulatory guidance (FDA, 2023; EMA, 2015). Yet trial datasets are rarely complete: baseline covariates can be missing, questionnaires may be only partly completed, and scheduled measurements may fall outside protocol windows. When baseline covariates planned for adjustment are incomplete, analysts must choose among several strategies-restricting to complete cases, applying simple deterministic rules (single imputation), using the missingness indicator method (MIM), or implementing multiple imputation (MI). The challenge intensifies when outcomes are also subject to missingness.
ICH E9(R1) underscores the importance of these choices by emphasizing alignment between the statistical analysis and the targeted estimand, and by cautioning against unnecessary alterations to the target population that arise from post hoc restrictions of the analysis set. Excluding participants solely because of missing baseline covariate data can inadvertently shift the population under analysis, complicating interpretation and reducing comparability across endpoints. As a result, there has been renewed interest in methods for handling missing covariates that preserve the integrity of the randomized population while remaining practical to implement.
This post focuses on a common confirmatory setting in which baseline covariates are included primarily to improve the precision of the estimated treatment effect. In that setting, the recent RCT-focused literature offers clearer guidance on which approaches perform well and which are best avoided.

title: Missing covariates in RCTs - what to do, what to avoid, and what to prespecify
text:
2.1 Multiple imputation (MI) when appropriate
Multiple imputation (MI) is widely used in confirmatory trials and is often a strong choice when missingness is non-trivial, particularly when several covariates are affected or when the data include a mix of continuous and categorical variables. MI preserves the intended analysis set and reflects imputation uncertainty through Rubin’s combining rules.
A widely accepted principle is that the imputation model should include all variables used in the analysis model and, where feasible, additional variables that are predictive of the missing covariate or of its missingness (the principle of congeniality between imputation and analysis models). When imputing baseline covariates only, treatment assignment should not be used as a predictor because by the randomization design it carries no information about the baseline covariate distribution; allowing arm-specific baseline imputations can also introduce chance treatment-group differences. The imputation model should instead include relevant baseline and design variables, such as stratification factors and site or region.
The computational burden of MIM is usually limited when only a small number of baseline covariates are imputed. It can become material when not only baseline covariates are imputed and the imputation model jointly covers many endpoints, visits, or variables in a large dataset. When outcomes are also subject to missingness, analysts sometimes consider performing MI in multiple sequential steps; in many settings, however, this can be avoided by specifying a single, jointly coherent imputation model that simultaneously handles missing covariates and missing outcomes (see Section 3).

title: Missing covariates in RCTs - what to do, what to avoid, and what to prespecify
section: 2.2 Missingness-indicator method (MIM): a simple option with RCT-specific
text:
2.2 Missingness-indicator method (MIM): a simple option with RCT-specific
support Zhao and Ding (2024) provide theoretical justification for the use of missingness indicators in randomized experiments when combined with an appropriate covariate-adjusted estimator. They show that, under randomization, the missingness indicator method (MIM) paired with Lin’s (2013) regression adjustment yields consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the average treatment effect, with potential precision gains, irrespective of the missing-data mechanism for the covariates. In practice, MIM replaces missing baseline covariate values with an arbitrary constant (commonly zero after centering, since the choice is absorbed by the indicator), augments the design matrix with the corresponding missingness indicators, and applies Lin-style regression adjustment (Lin et al. 2013)-including treatment-covariate interactions-with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. The procedure is straightforward to implement, retains all randomized participants in the analysis, and can improve precision relative to analyses that ignore partially observed covariates (Zhao and Ding, 2024).
Song, Hughes, and Ye (2024) offer a complementary efficiency-based perspective through their cross-world imputation framework, which clarifies the conditions under which MIM approximates an efficiency-optimal imputation strategy and how it relates to alternative imputation choices. From a practical standpoint, MIM is particularly appealing as a simple, prespecifiable analytic approach or as a sensitivity analysis, especially in settings where multiple imputation is operationally burdensome.

title: Missing covariates in RCTs - what to do, what to avoid, and what to prespecify
section: 2.3 Single imputation (mean, median, or mode): a pragmatic option requiring
text:
2.3 Single imputation (mean, median, or mode): a pragmatic option requiring
clear justification Single imputation is frequently criticized in the general missing-data literature because it does not naturally propagate imputation uncertainty, leading to underestimated standard errors and overly narrow confidence intervals (Little Rubin, 2019). The RCT-focused literature adds important nuance to this view. When covariates are used for adjustment in a randomized trial and the target estimand is the average treatment effect (ATE), simple imputation can yield valid inference (correct Type I error and CI coverage) when randomization is preserved, all randomized participants remain in the analysis, the imputations do not depend on treatment assignment or post-baseline outcomes, and the treatment effect is estimated with an appropriate covariate-adjusted estimator.. Moreover, Song, Hughes, and Ye (2024) show, within their efficiency-based framework, that certain simple imputation choices can approximate efficiency-optimal strategies for precision covariates. For example, if baseline age is used as an adjustment covariate and is missing for a small number of participants, a pre-specified mean imputation rule can preserve the full randomized analysis set and retain much of the precision benefit of covariate adjustment.
Therefore, in confirmatory settings single imputation could also be considered in primary analysis when missingness is minimal. When used, the rationale, the imputation rule, and its role within the analytic strategy should be prespecified and clearly justified in the statistical analysis plan.

title: Missing covariates in RCTs - what to do, what to avoid, and what to prespecify
section: 2.4 Complete-case covariate adjustment: generally not recommended
text:
2.4 Complete-case covariate adjustment: generally not recommended
Complete-case covariate adjustment is operationally simple but, on both theoretical and empirical grounds, is generally a suboptimal choice for the primary analysis of a randomized trial. By analyzing only participants with complete covariate data, this approach effectively focuses on a subset of the randomized population. As a result, estimating the ATE for all randomized participants requires additional assumptions beyond randomization (Zhao Ding, 2024).In addition, the reduction in effective sample size can lead to meaningful losses in precision. Simulation studies in RCT-like settings have reported notable efficiency losses and weaker overall performance for complete-case adjustment under realistic missingness patterns, relative to methods that retain the full randomized sample (Kayembe et al., 2022, 2024).
For these reasons, complete-case covariate adjustment is better positioned as a supplementary analysis rather than as the primary analytic strategy, except in settings where covariate missingness is negligible and plausibly unrelated to outcomes.

title: Covariate adjustment simulation studies
text:
When a sponsor wishes to include covariate adjustment in a trial protocol and statistical analysis plan, simulation studies can be useful both to select a covariate adjustment strategy and to justify to regulators that the selected strategy is appropriate. The questions that a simulation study can answer include:

Does the testing strategy appropriately control type I error under a range of assumptions regarding the distributions of the covariates and their relationship to the outcome?
Is the type I error rate adversely affected by using covariate adjustment in a group sequential design or by combining covariate adjustment with other adaptive trial design elements, e.g., information monitoring? (Tsiatis and Davidian, 2026; Van Lancker et al., 2025)
How will study power and the time to the conclusion of the study be affected by the covariate adjustment strategy, including which covariates are adjusted for (see companion blog of Alex Ocampo) and how missing data are handled (see companion blog of Jiawei Wei)?
How will covariate adjustment affect the properties of the treatment effect estimate?

title: Covariate adjustment simulation studies
text:
How to simulate
Trial elements to account for when carrying out a simulation study include:

The stratification factors, if any, and the randomization ratio and scheme that will be used, e.g., stratified permuted block randomization
The proposed adjustment set of covariate(s)
The design, including group sequential design elements
The number of patients, enrollment schedule and dropout rate
If the endpoint type is continuous, its distribution in the various study arms (mean, variance, etc.)
If the endpoint type is binary, its expected prevalence in the various study arms
If the endpoint type is ordinal, the prevalence of the various categories and whether proportional odds is assumed to hold
If the endpoint type is time-to-event, the baseline hazard function, whether proportional hazards is assumed to hold, the target number of events, etc.
Whether the model used for analysis will be correctly specified

Some considerations when specifying the relationship of covariates to the outcome include:

The expected prognostic strength of the covariate
Whether the relationship of covariates to the outcome is assumed to be the same across treatment arms
Whether the distribution of covariates of patients changes with enrollment time
In the case of time-to-event outcomes, whether and how the association between covariates and outcomes changes over time

When carrying out a simulation study, it is important to compare operating characteristics to unadjusted methods. Some quantities that can be compared include:

Standard errors (both their magnitude and whether they are consistent)
Rejection probabilities under null and alternative hypotheses
Bias in treatment effect estimates
Confidence interval coverage
Power

It is recommended to include Monte Carlo confidence intervals for these quantities. Many replicates may be required to show that rejection probabilities under the null are well controlled. When evaluating bias in treatment effect estimates, calculating the “true” value of the treatment effect may be challenging if it is a complicated function of the parameters used to design the simulation study. In this case, Monte Carlo simulation or numerical integration methods (Ocampo et al., 2026) may be used.
Although it is ideal for the simulation study to faithfully reflect aspects of the planned trial design, it may also be useful to simulate under different designs, e.g., it may be useful to simulate smaller or larger trials to further evaluate the finite sample size performance of the methods proposed to be used.
Note that special challenges may arise when designing a simulation study when a conditional estimand is used, as the estimand itself may change when covariate adjustment is used.
An alternative to simulation which may be more realistic as to the distribution of covariates and outcomes, but without incorporating all relevant features of a planned trial, is to resample from real trial data. For example, to evaluate the type I error rate of a method, we can use datasets repeatedly resampled from an actual trial with random assignment of treatment. This method will evaluate the type I error rate under a stricter null hypothesis than would normally be tested. For example, with time-to-event data, random assignment of treatment makes the censoring distribution identical between the arms, which may be unrealistic, and is not a required assumption for the log-rank test. It is more difficult to use resampling to study operating characteristics under a given alternative hypothesis. In this case, it may be useful to resample baseline covariates but simulate the outcome from a parametric model, see, e.g., Van Lancker et al. (2025).

title: Covariate adjustment simulation studies
text:
Case study
We use a planned metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) trial with overall survival (OS) as the primary endpoint as a case study to illustrate some features of a covariate adjustment simulation study and to illustrate the resampling approach mentioned above. Our aims are to assess whether the proposed analysis methods control the type I error rate for the planned trial design, whether the hazard ratio estimate will be unbiased and have the right confidence interval coverage, and how power depends on the prognostic power of the covariate. Here, we are interested in power gains but also in whether power will be lost if the covariate turns out to have no prognostic power.
We assume a median OS of 18 months in the control arm and a hazard ratio of 0.68 under the alternative. The trial uses an O’Brien-Fleming group sequential design with one interim analysis at 70% of information, 1:1 randomization, 2% annual dropout, and uniform enrollment over 12 months. We target 90% power at a two-sided significance level of 0.05. We assume that we are adjusting for one continuous covariate, which we assume is normally distributed.
The design requires 287 events at the final analysis; we round up to 300 events (interim at 210). We enroll 600 patients over 12 months.

Simulation setup
We simulate 600 patients enrolled uniformly over 12 months, with 2% annual dropout. Patients are assigned to one of four equally sized strata, and within each stratum treatment is assigned using 1:1 permuted block randomization with blocks of size 4. We adjust for a single continuous baseline covariate \(X_i \sim N(0,1)\). Event times are generated from a proportional hazards model
\[
h(t \mid X_i) = h_0(t) \exp(\beta X_i + \theta I_i),
\]
where \(I_i \in \{0,1\}\) is the treatment indicator, \(\theta = \log(\text{HR})\) is the log hazard ratio, and \(\beta\) controls the prognostic strength of the covariate. The only parameters we vary in this simulation study are \(\beta\) and \(\theta\). We set \(\beta \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}\) and consider \(\theta = 0\) (null) and \(\theta = \log(0.68)\) (alternative). The baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) is chosen so that event times are marginally exponentially distributed with median 18 months in the control arm, regardless of \(\beta\). This is achieved using the inverse cumulative hazard method (Bender et al., 2005). Event times are simulated separately for each combination of stratum and arm. We assume the stratification variable does not affect survival, i.e., strata membership is ignored when simulating the outcomes.
We evaluate the type I error rate of the unadjusted stratified log-rank test and the covariate-adjusted stratified log-rank test (Ye et al., 2024) at both the interim (210 events) and final (300 events) analyses, applying O’Brien-Fleming critical values. The covariate-adjusted stratified log-rank test tests exactly the same null hypothesis as the unadjusted stratified log-rank test. We evaluate the treatment effect using a stratified Cox proportional hazards model with only a term for treatment and also using the hazard ratio estimator under the stratified Cox proportional hazards model of Ye et al. (2024). The hazard ratio that is estimated is marginal with respect to the adjustment covariates. We evaluate its bias and the coverage of its confidence interval. We run 2,000,000 simulation replicates for each scenario. These covariate-adjusted methods are implemented in the R packages RobinCar and RobinCar2.

Resampling study
To evaluate the Type I error rate of the covariate-adjusted log-rank test in a realistic setting, we apply a bootstrap resampling approach to data from an actual mCRC trial (NCT00339183, available from Project Data Sphere).
For each replicate, patients are sampled with replacement from the trial data until the resampled dataset contains 300 events. Treatment labels are then randomly reassigned within each randomization stratum, replicating the stratified permuted block randomization used in the original trial. This enforces the strong null hypothesis — that each patient has the same hazard function under treatment and control — so any rejection of the null constitutes a type I error. The type I error rate is estimated over 500,000 replicates.
We evaluate three analysis strategies: the unadjusted log-rank test (LR), the covariate-adjusted log-rank test adjusting for the Bachet prognostic score (PS), and the covariate-adjusted log-rank test adjusting for the individual component variables of the Bachet score added one at a time (1 through 7 variables). The Bachet score (Bachet et al., 2025, Journal of Clinical Oncology) is a composite prognostic score for overall survival in mCRC derived from seven baseline variables: alkaline phosphatase, hemoglobin, ECOG PS, lactate dehydrogenase, absolute neutrophil count, number of metastatic sites, and platelet count. When the component variables are added one at a time they are added in the above order, which was determined using an independent mCRC trial dataset via a Cox proportional hazards model with a LASSO penalty.

As more individual component variables are added, the type I error rate increases. A small sample size correction (Krotka and Magirr, 2026) might be helpful to control the type I error rate when many variables are adjusted for.

title: Covariate Adjustment for Survival Endpoints in Randomized Clinical Trials
text:
Topic: Covariate Adjustment for Survival Endpoints in Randomized Clinical Trials
Datetime: May 8th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Presenter: Zhiwei Zhang is a senior director at Gilead Sciences. Before joining Gilead, he worked in academia and government agencies, including FDA and NIH. His research interests include causal inference and clinical trial design and analysis. Zhiwei has published over 100 research articles, mostly in statistical journals. He is an elected fellow of the American Statistical Association and the International Statistical Institute.
Summary: Covariate adjustment aims to improve the statistical efficiency of randomized trials by incorporating information from baseline covariates. Popular methods for covariate adjustment include analysis of covariance for continuous endpoints and standardized logistic regression for binary endpoints. For survival endpoints, while some covariate adjustment methods have been developed, they are not commonly used in practice for various reasons, including high demands for theoretical and methodological sophistication as well as computational skills. This talk describes two alternative methods: augmentation and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Both methods are simple, easy to understand and implement, and widely applicable to different effect measures. The augmentation method is available in an R package, and IPTW requires no special software. The methods are compared with existing methods in simulation studies and illustrated using real data from an HIV treatment trial.

title: Revealing the Truth: Calculating True Values in Causal Inference Simulation Studies via Gaussian Quadrature
text:
Topic: Revealing the Truth: Calculating True Values in Causal Inference Simulation Studies via Gaussian Quadrature
Datetime: March 13th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Presenter: Dr. Alex Ocampo is a Principal Statistical Methodologist at Roche.
Summary: Simulation studies are used to understand the properties of statistical methods. A key luxury in many simulation studies is knowledge of the true value (i.e. the estimand) being targeted. With this oracle knowledge in-hand, the researcher conducting the simulation study can assess across repeated realizations of the data how well a given method recovers the truth. In causal inference simulation studies, the truth is rarely a simple parameter of the statistical model chosen to generate the data. Instead, the estimand is often an average treatment effect, marginalized over the distribution of confounders and/or mediators. Luckily, these variables are often generated from common distributions such as the normal, uniform, exponential, or gamma. For all these distributions, Gaussian quadratures provide efficient and accurate calculation for integrands with integral kernels that stem from known probability density functions. We demonstrate through four applications how to use Gaussian quadrature to accurately and efficiently compute the true causal estimand. We also compare the pros and cons of Gauss-Hermite quadrature to Monte Carlo integration approaches, which we use as benchmarks. Overall, we demonstrate that the Gaussian quadrature is an accurate tool with negligible computation time, yet is underused for calculating the true causal estimands in simulation studies.

title: Practical considerations when using covariate-adjusted log-rank test, including adaptive designs
text:
Topic: Practical considerations when using covariate-adjusted log-rank test, including adaptive designs
Datetime: April 10th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Presenter: Dr. Daniel Backenroth is a Fellow of Biostatistics at Johnson & Johnson.
Summary: This talk will describe how the covariate-adjusted log-rank test can be used to enhance the power of late-phase oncology studies with primary time-to-event endpoints. Using as a case study a metastatic colorectal cancer trial with overall survival as the primary endpoint, we demonstrate how to use historical data to estimate variance reductions achievable through different covariate adjustment strategies, including adjustment for a prognostic score. We also compare these strategies with respect to Type I error rate control, and show via a simulation study that inflation arising from embedding covariate adjustment in a group sequential design can be avoided.
We also investigate adaptive designs that can be used to take advantage of increases in efficiency from the use of the covariate-adjusted log-rank test in trials with time-to-event endpoints. These adaptive designs are intended to address a key practical challenge in taking advantage of efficiency gains from this test, which is that the actual efficiency gain attained in a trial may differ from estimates of the efficiency gain at the design stage, and even from interim estimates during the trial.

title: Bias Reduction in G-Computation for Covariate Adjustment in Randomized Clinical Trials
text:
Topic: Bias Reduction in G-Computation for Covariate Adjustment in Randomized Clinical Trials
Datetime: Sep 4th Friday, 10am-11am ET.
Summary: G-computation is a powerful covariate adjustment method for analyzing randomized clinical trials. It typically relies on fitting canonical generalized linear models. However, this could be problematic when the sample size or event number is small relative to the number of covariates. Common issues include the underestimation of the variance and the potential nonexistence of maximum likelihood estimators. Bias reduction methods are commonly employed to address these issues, including Firth correction, which guarantees the existence of corresponding estimates. Yet, their application within g-computation remains underexplored. In this article, we analyze the asymptotic bias of g-computation estimators and propose a novel bias-reduction method that improves both estimation and inference. Our approach performs bias correction via generalized Oaxaca–Blinder estimators, and thus the resulting estimators are guaranteed to be bounded. The proposed debiased estimators use slightly modified versions of maximum likelihood or Firth correction estimators for nuisance parameters. We also introduce a simple small-sample bias adjustment for variance estimation to improve finite-sample inference validity. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our method offers superior finite-sample performance, effectively addressing the bias-efficiency tradeoff. Finally, we illustrate its practical utility by reanalyzing a completed randomized clinical trial. In this example, our method improves precision in a small subgroup analysis for which the standard method fails to fit the regression model. Recording:

title: Automated, efficient and model-free inference for randomized clinical trials via data-driven covariate adjustment
text:
Topic: Automated, efficient and model-free inference for randomized clinical trials via data-driven covariate adjustment
Datetime: September 13th Friday, 11am-12pm EDT.
Presenter: Kelly Van Lancker from Ghent University
Zoom link:: https://umich.zoom.us/j/7573650566
Summary: In May 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) released guidance for industry on “Adjustment for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products”. Covariate adjustment is a statistical analysis method for improving precision and power in clinical trials by adjusting for pre-specified, prognostic baseline variables. Though recommended by the FDA and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), many trials do not exploit the available information in baseline variables or make use only of the baseline measurement of the outcome. This is likely (partly) due to the regulatory mandate to pre-specify baseline covariates for adjustment, leading to challenges in determining appropriate covariates and their functional forms. We will explore the potential of automated data-adaptive methods, such as machine learning algorithms, for covariate adjustment, addressing the challenge of pre-specification. Specifically, our approach allows the use of complex models or machine learning algorithms without compromising the interpretation or validity of the treatment effect estimate and its corresponding standard error, even in the presence of misspecified outcome working models. This contrasts the majority of competing works which assume correct model specification for the validity of standard errors. Our proposed estimators either necessitate ultra-sparsity in the outcome model (which can be relaxed by limiting the number of predictors in the model) or necessitate integration with sample splitting to enhance their performance. As such, we will arrive at simple estimators and standard errors for the marginal treatment effect in randomized clinical trials, which exploit data-adaptive outcome predictions based on prognostic baseline covariates, and have low (or no) bias in finite samples even when those predictions are themselves biased.

title: Finite-sample correction for the covariate-adjusted log-rank test
text:
Topic: Finite-sample correction for the covariate-adjusted log-rank test
Datetime: Dec 11th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Abstract: The covariate-adjusted log-rank test is a novel method for covariate adjustment in randomized trials with time-to-event endpoints, offering guaranteed efficiency gains compared to the standard log-rank test. However, it has been noted that, in small samples, this method may lead to type I error rate inflation. This issue is particularly pronounced in trials with imbalanced allocation and settings where the number of adjustment covariates is large relative to the sample size. We propose a finite-sample correction for the denominator of the covariate-adjusted log-rank test statistic that accounts for the loss of the residual degrees of freedom as well as the uncertainty in the unknown regression coefficients. In simulations, we show that applying this correction leads to a substantial reduction in the type I error rate inflation across multiple scenarios.

title: Improving Variance Estimation for Covariate Adjustment with Binary Outcomes
text:
Topic: Improving Variance Estimation for Covariate Adjustment with Binary Outcomes
Datetime: Nov 13th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Abstract: Covariate adjustment is a general method for improving precision when estimating treatment effects in randomized trials and is recommended by the FDA in its 2023 guidance when baseline variables are prognostic for the primary outcome. We focus on a method highlighted in that guidance called standardization" (org-computation”) for estimating the marginal treatment effect. We address the question of how to reliably estimate variance for binary outcomes when marginal outcome probabilities are close to 0 or 1. We propose an influence function-based leave-one-out cross-validated (IF-LOO) variance estimator for the standardized difference-in-means average treatment effect. Through simulation studies, we show that this estimator provides appropriate type-I error control and performs reliably in challenging settings where existing methods can yield inflated type-I error or fail entirely, such as when outcome events are rare or sample sizes are small. In addition to having desirable statistical properties, we derive a closed-form expression for the proposed estimator, enabling straightforward and reliable implementation by study statisticians. The robust finite-sample performance and ease of implementation suggest the IF-LOO variance estimator is a prudent default choice for standardization in clinical trials.

title: Increasing the efficiency of randomized trials with machine learning

Topic: Increasing the efficiency of randomized trials with machine learning
Datetime: Nov 14th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Presenter: Dr. Alejandro Schuler is an Assistant Professor in Residence at UC Berkeley Biostatistics. His research focus is on developing methods for clinical decision-making in the real world that are economically or clinically necessary, statistically rigorous, and frictionless from the user perspective.
Summary: Trials enroll a large number of subjects in order to attain power, making them expensive and time-consuming. However, advancements in machine learning can make adjusted trial analyses more efficient, yielding smaller confidence intervals and p-values without sacrificing control of false positives. Adjustment works by explaining away within-treatment-group variability in the outcome using associated variability in baseline covariates. Therefore, the key parameter that determines power and confidence of an adjusted analysis is how predictive the baseline covariates are for the outcome. Machine learning models often predict better than linear models and therefore they boost power. Historical data can also be used to improve predictions and it is possible to do so without incurring bias. The power gain is predictable if we can accurately anticipate model performance, which allows us to trade power gains with the same sample size for smaller trials with equal power.

title: Bridging Balancing Weights and Augmentation in Covariate-adjusted Analyses with Time-to-Event Endpoints: Theory and Practical Recommendations
text:
Topic: Bridging Balancing Weights and Augmentation in Covariate-adjusted Analyses with Time-to-Event Endpoints: Theory and Practical Recommendations
Datetime: Jan 8th Friday, 11am-12pm ET.
Abstract: Covariate adjustment improves the efficiency of treatment-effect analyses in randomized clinical trials, provided the adjustment targets the correct quantity. For time-to-event endpoints, two marginal targets are of primary interest: the log-rank test for the presence of a treatment effect and the marginal hazard ratio for its magnitude. Existing covariate adjustment approaches reach these targets by different ways. Augmentation adjusts the log-rank score by regressing derived outcomes on the baseline covariates within each arm. Weighting instead reweights the two arms to balance the covariates before the survival comparison is formed: inverse probability weighting does so through a fitted propensity model, while calibration weighting solves directly for weights that match covariate means. In this manuscript, we first develop balancing weighting for time-to-event endpoints, covering both calibration weights (stable balancing weights and entropy balancing) and propensity score weights, and prove that any balancing-regular weighting is first-order equivalent to the augmented log-rank score and to the root of the marginal Cox score. All three routes therefore deliver the same estimator to first order, and calibration reaches it without fitting any model. The weighted procedures thereby inherit the validity and guaranteed efficiency gain of the augmentation approach. In addition, we show that the efficiency gain grows with the prognostic strength of the adjustment covariates, while the practical caveat lies in variance estimation, for which we give recommendations to guard against finite-sample Type I error inflation. We further confirm our results through simulation studies and an analysis of the REWIND cardiovascular trial.

title: Advancement Subteam
text:
The overarching goal of the advance sub-team is to develop and disseminate new statistical methods that address emerging challenges in covariate adjustment for randomized clinical trials (RCTs).
In the past five years, covariate adjustment has become increasing popular in analyzing RCTs and has also attracted great attention for methodological developments. However, the increasing complexities of real-world RCTs has outpaced the method development, leaving tons of open questions regarding covariate adjustment. For example, it remains not fully clear about the benefit of covariate adjustment and its appropriate implementation given missing data, longitudinal outcomes, time-to-event outcomes, complex trial designs, etc. These important gaps between practice and theory demand continuing efforts to deepen our understanding and develop new tools. As the statistical practice evolves, the advance sub-team aims to stay in the frontline of new techniques, results, and tools, targeting the boundary of knowledge and unopened questions.
Bearing the aim, the advance sub-team plans two kinds of activities:

A monthly journal club to communicate new results regarding covariate adjustment.
An online forum for group-members to post/discuss questions and share resources.



The journal club takes an online format via zoom meeting and welcomes all members of the working group. Depending on the public interest, external audience can be accommodated later.
The journal club can take two formats: (1) roundtable discussion of an issue/question raised by group members; or (2) a seminar of recent papers presented by group members or invited external speakers. All sub-team members are encouraged to bring up roundtable topics and papers of interest through a shared Google doc, and Dr. Bingkai Wang will tentatively take the responsibilities to make schedule, invite and host speakers, and lead discussion. We do not restrict the topic of each meeting as long as it is relevant to covariate adjustment, e.g., a new method, confusions about current results, statistical software, experience sharing, etc. For each journal club meeting, we expect a warm and in-depth discussion such that new thoughts and results can be freely communicated.



The online forum serves as a platform for group members to share news, discuss questions, and post resources. In the early stage, a simple Google doc will be used to realize this function, and a formal webpage will be developed later. Dr. Bingkai Wang will tentatively maintain the forum and draft monthly newsletters summarizing the discussions for all group members.
We anticipate an informal and friendly forum that puts no pressure in speaking and benefits all readers. The sub-team members are especially encouraged to post thoughts and responses through the forum, aiming to warm up the forum in the early stage.
Beyond the two activities,we also encourage offline collaborations and connections. We believe the planned activities can be a valuable opportunity to nurture new thoughts, connections, and findings. As a working group gathering worldwide talents and experts of RCTs, we have no doubt on the potential value of this platform and look forward to its powerful impact on the community.
